title: A Heat Wave Is Sweeping the US as the World Cup Kicks Off. South Asians Are Uniquely at Risk.
excerpt: More than 200,000 heat deaths in Europe since 2022. A scorching American summer ahead. And a diaspora population that thinks it knows heat but is dangerously wrong about this kind.
body:
The first sustained heat wave of the American summer arrived this week. Temperatures across the Southeast are pushing past 100 degrees Fahrenheit, heat advisories blanket a dozen states, and the National Weather Service is warning that this early-season heat is more dangerous precisely because bodies have not yet acclimatised.

This is also the week the FIFA World Cup began on American soil.

The collision of these two events creates a specific danger for the Indian diaspora — one that most NRIs do not adequately recognise. Tens of thousands of desi fans are expected at World Cup venues across the country this summer, many of them in outdoor or semi-outdoor stadiums in cities where heat indices will regularly exceed 105°F. And for families who have flown in elderly parents from India for summer visits, the risk is compounded in ways that deserve urgent attention.

## The Numbers Are Not Abstract

The World Health Organization released new data this week showing that extreme heat has killed more than 200,000 people across Europe since 2022. Hans Henri Kluge, the WHO's Europe director, called heat "a silent killer" and noted that most of these deaths were "entirely preventable."

The casualties are overwhelmingly concentrated among the elderly, people with cardiovascular disease, kidney problems, and diabetes — conditions that disproportionately affect South Asians. A 2024 study in *The Lancet Planetary Health* found that South Asian populations face elevated heat-related mortality risk even at lower temperature thresholds than European populations, partly due to higher baseline rates of metabolic syndrome.

For NRIs, this intersects with a common summer pattern: elderly parents visiting from India for months-long stays. Many of these visitors arrive assuming that because they survived Indian summers, American heat poses no special threat. This assumption is dangerous.

## Why Indian Heat Tolerance Does Not Transfer

The heat in Chennai or Nagpur is brutal but culturally managed. Homes are often designed with cross-ventilation. Activity slows in the afternoon. Hydration habits — from nimbu pani to buttermilk — are ingrained. The body acclimatises over weeks.

American heat is different. Humidity levels in the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic can push heat indices far beyond what the thermostat reads. Air-conditioned interiors create massive temperature differentials when stepping outside. And the social expectation to remain active — attending a grandson's soccer match, walking through a shopping complex parking lot, sitting in a World Cup stadium for three hours — overrides the instinctive caution that Indian heat enforces.

Elderly visitors are also often reluctant to drink sufficient water ("I don't feel thirsty"), resistant to wearing hats or sunscreen ("I never needed it in India"), and unfamiliar with the symptoms of heat exhaustion as distinct from general fatigue.

## At the World Cup: Specific Precautions

FIFA and local health authorities have already flagged heat risk for spectators. Several venues, including those in Dallas, Houston, Miami and Atlanta, will see game-day temperatures above 95°F during the group stage. Medical tents and hydration stations will be available, but the walk from parking to seats, the time spent in security queues, and the duration of the match itself all represent sustained heat exposure.

Doctors recommend the following for anyone attending a match or spending extended time outdoors this summer:

- **Pre-hydrate** with water or electrolyte drinks at least two hours before going outside. Thirst is a lagging indicator; by the time you feel it, dehydration has already begun.
- **Wear light, loose-fitting clothing** and a hat. Moisture-wicking fabrics reduce the body's cooling burden.
- **Know the warning signs.** Heavy sweating, thirst, and fatigue are early signals. Dizziness, headache, nausea and confusion are escalations that require immediate action: stop activity, move to shade, apply cold compresses, and call for help.
- **Heat stroke is a medical emergency.** When the body's temperature rises above 106°F, confusion gives way to loss of consciousness. Call 911 immediately. Apply ice or cold wet cloths. Do not wait to see if it passes.
- **Check on elderly family members** every few hours during heat advisories. A phone call is not enough — visit in person if possible, especially if they live in homes without reliable air conditioning.

## The Broader Pattern

Climate scientists have made clear that heat waves are growing longer, more frequent, and more intense. The WHO's Europe report is a preview of what the American healthcare system will face in the decades ahead. For a diaspora community with elevated baseline cardiovascular and metabolic risk, this is not a one-summer problem.

The practical message is simple: treat American summer heat with the same respect you would treat a blizzard or a hurricane. It is a weather event that kills, and the people most at risk are often the least likely to recognise the danger until it is too late.

**Sources:** World Health Organization (June 2026); CNN Health; National Weather Service; *The Lancet Planetary Health*
